questions.questionText: A model gets 55% accuracy on training data and 54% on test data. What does this suggest?
options: High bias (underfitting) — the model is too simple to capture the pattern even on data it trained on
The test set is too small to draw any conclusion
questions.correctAnswer: High bias (underfitting) — the model is too simple to capture the pattern even on data it trained on
questions.explanation: Similar (and both low) train and test accuracy indicates the model isn't even fitting the training data well — a hallmark of underfitting, not overfitting.

questions.questionText: Why is it invalid to evaluate a model's performance using the same data it was trained on?
options: It's not invalid, training accuracy is the best measure of quality
The model may have memorized that specific data, so training accuracy doesn't reflect how well it generalizes to new data
Training accuracy is always lower than test accuracy
questions.correctAnswer: The model may have memorized that specific data, so training accuracy doesn't reflect how well it generalizes to new data
questions.explanation: A model can achieve perfect training accuracy purely by memorizing noise, which tells you nothing about how it will perform on data it hasn't seen — hence the need for a held-out test set.

questions.questionText: According to the bias-variance tradeoff, what typically happens when you increase a model's complexity (e.g. deeper trees, smaller k)?
options: Both bias and variance decrease together
Bias tends to decrease while variance tends to increase
Neither bias nor variance is affected by complexity
Bias tends to increase while variance tends to decrease
questions.correctAnswer: Bias tends to decrease while variance tends to increase
questions.explanation: A more complex model can fit more intricate patterns (lower bias) but also becomes more sensitive to noise in the specific training set it saw (higher variance) — you can't minimize both simultaneously by complexity alone.
